doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The Half Note recordings with Marsh and Bill Evans
summary: They discuss Revelation's edited release, the late CD release, and Bill Evans comping little for Konitz.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: Do you want to tell the tale about that? When Lennie released that on Revelation Records in the seventies with your solos cut out? What was that about?

It was about getting to hear Warne and study Warne for the students of Warne’s playing, obviously. When I heard it certainly I was offended that I was linking before or after, but I appreciated that. I wanted to study his solos also. That’s a great way to just have a series of solos end to end.
So what he did was not originally intended to be put out as a record I take it?
I don’t know that.

Because Revelation Records released it that way in the seventies. The way the music was actually recorded didn’t come out on CD until the nineties with that two CD set called Lee Konitz at the Half Note.
It was recorded in fifty-nine?
Yeah.
And released in the nineties?
Yeah. I have the two CD set. It was in the can all those years.
Holy shit.
You’ve heard those things right?
Yeah.
How did you feel about that situation? Were you comfortable with that?

I loved that. I was a little bit disturbed that Bill was not terribly comfortable and not comping for me especially a lot and I concluded after close listening that I was sharp to the piano and that’s possibly the reason. But I don’t thing he comped for Warne a lot either.
He did, yeah.
He did comp for Warne?
Yeah, consistently. But almost nothing for you which is really curious.
Yeah.
And you sound fine. You don’t sound “sharp” or anymore so than you . . .
A couple times when he did come in I felt the upper register a little bit conflicting.
But everybody plays great on it.
Twenty-one years between the recording and the release. Thirty-one.
Yeah. It came out in the mid-nineties.
Wow.
Yeah like ninety-four, ninety-five. I remember when it first came out. But as I understand it that was normally Tristano’s gig?

Apparently he took off Tuesday nights to finish his teaching thing. I don’t know how many weeks we were there to make a special situation like that where we had to have a special night off to see his students.
He took his teaching seriously.
Well obviously. But I think Bill was a little uncomfortable in that role but he does some great playing on that record.
He does indeed.
So that’s the final litmus test.
You and Warne sound as good together as you always did.
